name: Mohair velvet (cut warp pile of mohair on a cotton or mohair-cotton ground)
summary: A warp-pile cloth: an extra warp woven into a ground cloth and cut, so a dense short pile of fibre ends stands up from it. The Salon's backless benches in bays 2-5 are upholstered in velvet of each bay's colour. This record proposes mohair for the pile, the contract-seating choice for wear, lustre and inherent fire performance; the Architect may choose cotton or silk instead.

formation.how: Velvet is woven as two cloths face to face, joined by an extra pile warp that passes between them (or over rods and wires); cutting the pile warp between the layers gives two lengths of fabric, each with a dense, even pile of cut ends. Mohair is the hair of the Angora goat: its scales are not fully developed as wool's are, so it is smooth and lustrous, takes dye well, and is durable, elastic, crease-resistant and flame-resistant.

weaving.text: Two thicknesses of the material are woven simultaneously, connected with an extra warp yarn woven over rods or wires, then separated by cutting.

asperityScattering.text: A layer of sparse scatterers (hairs, dust) adds a surface lobe to the diffuse, backscatter and specular lobes: low except when the light or the view grazes the surface, so it brightens an object's outline and dominates the look of velvet.

conservation.keratin: Mohair is a keratin fibre like wool: it is food for clothes-moth and carpet-beetle larvae, and wool in contact has blackened brass (see wool-felt). The benches carry no metal against the cloth.

sensitivity.text: High light sensitivity (ISO Blue Wool 1-3) covers most plant extracts and hence most historic bright dyes, insect dyes, most early synthetic colours, and textiles; UV causes yellowing, chalking and weakening, and prolonged exposure weakens and fragments most wool, cotton, silk and paper.
